description: Multidisciplinary team of 3 working on Field Shift: helping small farmers in rural Mexico choose what and when to plant, using NASA satellite data and local records. Aquiles: predictions and app. José Ángel: backend systems. Lesly Paola: data collection and cleaning.
summary:
Milpa Clara is a mobile-friendly web app that helps rainfed farmers decide when to sow and harvest. In Mexico, 72% of farmland depends on rain alone (INEGI, 2025), and planting too early or too late can cost the harvest. Users answer five simple questions and get a plan: for each activity, a recommended date, a window of good days, a confidence level and a plain-language reason, downloadable as a PDF that works offline. Amealquito, an on-screen guide, walks them through each step.

The method works for any NASA POWER grid cell: it combines over two decades of NASA POWER rainfall and temperature, MODIS NDVI and HLS imagery with local harvest records (SIAP), drought monitoring (CONAGUA), soil data and FAO-56 crop water needs to find when the rains usually become established and how often that held. We validated it in a pilot zone in central Mexico, where every one of the six worst maize years since 2003 fell in a season NASA measured as drier than the median. The app accepts any of Mexico’s 2,478 municipalities and says plainly when a zone has no data yet. We also trained an LSTM to forecast NDVI; it did not beat the historical average, so the app says so and uses the simpler method. The tool supports the farmer’s decision; it does not replace it.
details:
What it does and how it works

Milpa Clara is a mobile-friendly web app, in Spanish, that helps rainfed farmers decide when to sow and harvest. Users answer five questions, one per screen: what they grow (maize, beans or oats), where they farm (any of Mexico’s 2,478 municipalities, typed or by GPS), whether the place on the map is right, how many years they have farmed, and what they want help with (a better harvest, using less water, or earning more). Amealquito, an on-screen guide, explains each step.

The plan shows, for each activity (sowing, fertilizing, harvest), a recommended date, a window of good days, a confidence level and a one-line reason with its source. Confidence is how often that window held in past seasons, such as “in 15 of 23 seasons, the rains became established in these days.” The plan also lists the bad years the farmer lived through and adds one card for each priority: crop risk, water per crop cycle or income per hectare. It downloads as a one- or two-page PDF with the same content as the screen, generated offline. A section called “Can you trust these dates?” compares our models openly, and a full study page keeps the multi-year analysis, maps and crop comparisons.

Each zone with data covers a radius of 25 km, about half a NASA POWER grid cell. If a place falls outside every zone, the app says so, shows the distance to the nearest one, and offers that zone’s plan only as a clearly marked reference. All numbers are precomputed into JSON files with their source and query date. The site never calls NASA services live, so it works on a weak connection. When a value is missing, it says “no data” instead of guessing.

Data and validation

  • NASA POWER daily rainfall, temperature, radiation, humidity and reference evapotranspiration (2000–2026).
  • MODIS MOD13A1 NDVI, with a cropland mask from MCD12Q1 land cover.
  • SRTM elevation.
  • HLS imagery through NASA GIBS and CMR.
  • Municipal harvest records (SIAP), the drought monitor (CONAGUA), soil data (SoilGrids), FAO-56 crop coefficients and the INEGI municipal catalog.

We validated the method in a pilot zone in central Mexico, checking the satellite data against what happened in the field: all six of the worst maize years in 2003–2025 fell in seasons that NASA POWER measured as drier than the median (Fisher’s exact test, p = 0.0046).

Machine learning, honestly reported

We trained an LSTM (2 layers, 64 units, 5 seeds) to forecast late-season NDVI from April–July inputs. The data was split by year: training 2001–2017, validation 2018–2020, test 2021–2025. We compared it with the historical average, Ridge regression, Random Forest and a GRU. The historical average won on validation, and the LSTM did not beat it on the test years (skill −0.016). Random Forest did better on the test years but worse on validation, so we did not pick it. The app says all this, and the calendar uses the simpler, validated method.

Benefits and intended impact

In Mexico, 72% of farmland depends on rain alone (INEGI, 2025), so sowing is the farmer’s biggest yearly bet: plant too early and the seed can be lost; plant too late and the crop may not mature before the frost. NASA has measured rainfall everywhere for decades, but it reaches farmers as raw data, not as a date. Milpa Clara turns those records into a decision a farmer can check: when to plant, how sure it is and why. It is designed for farmers and for the extension workers and family members who help them with a phone. It supports the farmer’s own judgment; it does not replace it.

Creativity

  • We test every recommendation against past seasons before it is shown. In the pilot zone, a tempting rule, “switch to oats if the rains are late,” lost $4,048/ha over 2003–2025 compared with always planting maize, so we removed it.
  • Negative results stay visible, including our own model’s.
  • Every number carries its source, its scale (from 30 m pixels to ~55 km cells or a municipality) and its confidence.
  • The app refuses to pass off another zone’s dates as the user’s own.

Tools

  • Website: HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, a static site with no login; jsPDF for offline PDFs.
  • Data scripts: Python.
  • Models: Google Colab with PyTorch.
  • Collaboration: Git and GitHub.
  • AI assistance: Claude Code (see “Use of AI”).

Factors we considered

  • Scale: rainfall comes in ~55 km cells, so the data describes the zone, not the plot.
  • Coverage: today the pilot zone is the only one with data; adding a zone means repeating the same precomputed steps for its grid cell.
  • Questionable records: official harvest data sometimes reports no losses in dry years, so we cross-check it with NASA rainfall.
  • Climate trend: in the pilot zone, maximum temperature has risen 0.53 °C per decade, and early frost hit 6 of 23 seasons.
  • Connectivity: rural internet is weak, so everything is precomputed and works without live calls.
  • Phones: it is designed for mobile screens.
  • Privacy: there is no login, and location is used only on the phone, never stored or sent.
  • The farmer decides: the app explains; the decision stays with the farmer.
